text: Something tedious is boring in a slow, dragging way — not hard, just dull and repetitive enough to make you want to stop. The article opens with the word on purpose: plain exercise works perfectly well, but it is so tedious that people give it up, and that is the problem VR games might solve.

Sedentary means sitting still, with little or no movement. Scientists usually use it for a whole way of living rather than one afternoon — a sedentary job, a sedentary lifestyle. Here it labels the comparison game, the one you play without ever leaving your chair.

Vigorous means done with a lot of energy and force. In this article it is not an opinion but a measurement: anything above six METs counts as vigorous exercise, however easy it happens to feel. Elsewhere the word stretches to a vigorous argument or a vigorous shake of a bottle.

Taxing here has nothing to do with money or taxes. It means demanding — something that drains your energy and takes real effort. Playing in a VR headset with a controller in each hand can be taxing because you are squatting, dodging and punching the whole time.

A caveat is a warning or a condition attached to an answer — the “but” that stops a simple yes from being the whole truth. The article says VR counts as real exercise “though with caveats,” and then spends the rest of the piece listing them: some games barely raise your heart rate, and none of them build strength.

To evaluate something is to judge how good, big or effective it is, usually by measuring rather than guessing. One way to evaluate VR exercise is the MET scale, which turns a vague question into a number you can compare.

To expend something is to use it up. It is most often used for energy, effort or money. A body at rest expends about one MET, meaning that is the amount of fuel it burns just staying alive and doing nothing.

Metabolic describes anything to do with metabolism — the chemical process by which your body turns food into the energy it runs on. It is the first word in “metabolic equivalent of task,” because that scale measures how fast your body is burning fuel during an activity.

Here “proper” does not mean polite or correct. In British English it often means real or genuine — the actual thing rather than a weak version of it. Asking whether VR games count as proper exercise means asking whether they are real exercise, not just something that resembles it.

This is not the “determined” that means stubborn and refusing to give up. In science writing, to determine something is to find it out for certain by testing. Researchers determined that one boxing game was a 9.3 MET activity, meaning they measured it and settled the number.

A mode is one particular way of doing something. In a video game, modes are the different settings or styles you can choose to play in. “Flow” and “Boxing” are two modes inside the game Supernatural, and the study measured them separately because they demand different amounts of effort.

Participants are the people who take part in something — in science, the volunteers being studied. The participants in the 2024 study each played a sitting-down game, two VR games, and walked on a treadmill, ten minutes apiece, while researchers measured their breathing.

Intensity is how strong, hard or concentrated something is. For exercise it means how hard your body is working, not how long you keep going. The article's key finding is that intensity varies more between one VR game and another than it does between virtual sport and the real thing.

Adolescents are young people in the years between childhood and adulthood — roughly ages ten to nineteen. The weight-loss study used 227 of them, which makes its results especially relevant to anyone reading this handout.

In everyday speech significant just means important. In science it has a stricter job: a significant difference is one large enough that it almost certainly did not happen by chance. Saying there was no significant difference between the real and virtual groups means the gap was small enough to be random noise.

Variation is the amount of difference within a group of things. The sentence is making a careful point: the variation between individual VR games is bigger than the variation between virtual and real exercise, so which game you pick matters more than whether it is virtual at all.

Resistance is a force pushing back against you. Muscles grow by working against it, which is why weights and resistance machines build strength. A virtual barbell has no weight and pushes back with nothing, so no matter how hard you swing at it, your muscles get no resistance to fight.

To augment something is to add to it to make it better or more powerful. The UCLA researchers augmented an ordinary cable weight machine by bolting on a VR headset, so real pulldowns and deadlifts became attacks in a game.

Endurance is the ability to keep going for a long time without wearing out. It is different from strength, which is how much force you can produce at once. The VR group improved in both, plus peak leg power.

Exertion is physical effort — how hard you are actually working your body. The striking result here is that people got their exertion level wrong: they judged it to be lower than it really was, because the game held their attention instead of the effort.

To perceive something is to notice it or judge it through your senses. What you perceive can be different from what is true, which is exactly the point being made: the lifters perceived their exertion to be lower than it actually was.

To underestimate something is to guess it is smaller, weaker or easier than it really is. People exercising in VR consistently underestimate how hard they are working — which may be the most useful thing about it, since the work still counts even when it does not feel like work.

Conventional means usual, ordinary, done the standard way. Conventional exercise here means the normal kind — running, lifting, a gym class — as opposed to strapping on a headset. People report finding the VR version more fun than the conventional one.

This is not a trial in a courtroom. In science a trial is a carefully run test that compares groups to find out whether something really works — the same word used for drug trials. The last line jokes that you do not need a formal trial to know that some exercise beats none.

To assess something is to measure or judge it carefully. The article's closing complaint is that most VR exercise studies are too small and lack proper comparisons, so their real effects cannot be assessed — nobody can tell how much the games actually did.

MET is short for metabolic equivalent of task, a scale for how hard an activity makes your body work. One MET is a body sitting still, so every other number is a multiple of doing nothing: walking is three METs, football is ten, and six is the line above which exercise counts as vigorous.

VR stands for virtual reality: a headset covering your eyes that shows a computer-made world, with hand controllers that track how you move so you can punch, slice or aim inside it. Because your whole body moves to play, some VR games turn out to be real exercise.

A control group is the group in an experiment that gets nothing, or gets the ordinary treatment, so the other groups have something to be compared against. Here the fifth group of teenagers played no sport at all and lost no weight — which is the only reason the 5kg the other groups lost can be credited to the sport rather than to growing up.

Cardio is short for cardiovascular exercise — the kind that raises your heart rate and makes you breathe harder, training your heart and lungs. Running, swimming and cycling are cardio; lifting heavy weights slowly is not. “So much for cardio” means the article is done with that half of the question and turning to weight loss.

Aerobic means with oxygen. Aerobic exercise is steady work your body fuels by breathing harder, which is why researchers measure oxygen consumption to gauge it. Saying the boxing game was comparable in aerobic intensity to a treadmill walk means both made the body pull in a similar amount of air.

A tower-defence game is a type of video game where waves of enemies advance toward a base you have to protect, and you fight them off from a fixed position. UCLA used one because the player can stay planted at a weight machine, turning each pulldown into an attack.

“So much for X” signals that the writer is finished with one topic and moving on to the next. It can also mean a hope has been disappointed, as in “so much for our picnic” when it rains. Here it is the first, friendlier sense: enough about cardio, now on to weight loss.

“All that said” introduces a final point that survives every objection just listed. The writer has spent paragraphs on doubts — small studies, missing comparisons — and then uses this phrase to say that despite all of it, one simple thing is still true: VR exercise beats no exercise.

“Not all X are created equal” is a set phrase meaning the members of a group differ in quality and should not be lumped together. It echoes the American Declaration of Independence, where “all men are created equal” means something far more serious. Here it simply warns that one VR game can be a workout while another barely counts.

To work up a sweat is to exercise hard enough that you actually start sweating — everyday proof that your body is working. Adding “a real sweat” insists it is genuine, which matters when the exercise in question is happening inside a video game.

To get around a problem is to find a clever way past it rather than solving it head-on. VR cannot provide real resistance, so instead of trying to make virtual weights heavy, the UCLA team got around it by attaching the headset to a real weight machine.
